sec.title: Background
sec.p: Infigratinib, an oral fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) 1-3 inhibitor, showed clinical activity and manageable adverse events in the P2 CBGJ398X2204 study and was conditionally approved for adults with previously treated, unresectable, or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) with FGFR2 fusion or other rearrangement. PROOF 301, reported in this article, is the confirmatory phase III trial of infigratinib versus gemcitabine plus cisplatin as first-line treatment of FGFR2-rearranged CCA.

sec.title: Patients and methods
sec.p: Eligible adult patients were randomly assigned in a 2 : 1 ratio to infigratinib 125 mg on days 1-21 of a 28-day treatment cycle versus gemcitabine (1000 mg/m2) + cisplatin (25 mg/m2) on days 1 and 8 of a 21-day cycle. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included overall survival, investigator-determined PFS, overall response rate (ORR), best overall response, disease control rate, duration of response, and safety.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Over 40 months, 1127 patients were pre-screened at 120 sites, and 48 patients were randomly allocated to the study in a 2 : 1 ratio (29 to infigratinib, 19 to chemotherapy). With a target accrual of ∼300 patients, this study was terminated early due to poor accrual. Median PFS (95% confidence interval) by blinded independent central review (BICR) was 7.4 and 8.0 months with infigratinib and chemotherapy, respectively. The ORRs by BICR were 37.9% with infigratinib and 15.8% with chemotherapy. Grade 3-4 adverse events occurred in 79.3% and 58.8% patients treated with infigratinib and chemotherapy, respectively.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Early termination limited the ability to draw definitive conclusions on the efficacy of infigratinib as first-line treatment of FGFR2-rearranged CCA. This study illustrates the challenges of powering confirmatory studies in biomarker-selected subpopulations of rare tumors and highlights the need for regulatory collaboration to develop pragmatic frameworks for assessing novel therapies in ultra-rare malignancies.

list-item.p: The PROOF 301 trial of infigratinib versus chemotherapy in FGFR2-rearranged CCA was terminated early due to poor accrual.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is a rare, heterogeneous malignancy originating from the intrahepatic biliary tree and accounting for 10%-20% of cases of cholangiocarcinoma.1 Approximately two-thirds of patients with cholangiocarcinoma are diagnosed at an advanced stage with unresectable or metastatic disease.2 For these patients, the standard of care for over a decade has been gemcitabine plus cisplatin, which significantly increased progression-free survival (PFS) in the ABC-02 trial,1,3,4 while the median overall survival was 11.7 months in the combination group. More recently, the TOPAZ-1 trial indicated that durvalumab plus combination chemotherapy improved survival in advanced biliary tract cancer (BTC), showing a median overall survival of 12.8 months for the durvalumab plus gemcitabine and cisplatin group and 11.5 months in the comparator arm.5 These results led to durvalumab plus gemcitabine and cisplatin being recommended as the preferred first-line therapy by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network Guidelines for Biliary Tract Cancers.6 Similarly, the KEYNOTE-966 trial showed that adding pembrolizumab to gemcitabine and cisplatin provided a survival advantage.7

Comprehensive genomic profiling identified multiple molecular aberrations in BTC, leading to a paradigm shift toward targeted therapies in cholangiocarcinoma.8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 The fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) 1-4 family plays an important role in cholangiocarcinoma pathology,14 with FGFR rearrangements occurring in 9%-16% of cases,9,13,15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 highlighting it as a potential target for therapy.9 Recently, an incidence of 3% of FGFR2 rearrangements was assessed in the TOPAZ-1 trial, which included patients with either intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, or gall-bladder carcinoma.21

Infigratinib (formerly known as BGJ398, BBP-831, and infigratinib phosphate), an orally bioavailable, potent, and selective adenosine triphosphate-competitive tyrosine kinase inhibitor of FGFR1-3, has demonstrated antitumor activity in non-clinical in vitro and in vivo tumor models harboring FGFR alterations.22,23 Phase I studies identified a maximum tolerated dose of 125 mg/day, 3 weeks on/1 week off, in 28-day cycles.24 The phase II study CBGJ398X2204 (hereafter referred to as Study 2204; NCT02150967) in a previously treated advanced cholangiocarcinoma setting demonstrated clinically meaningful antitumor activity, with blinded independent central review (BICR)-confirmed overall response rate and disease control in 23% and 84% of patients with FGFR2 rearrangements, respectively.25 The median duration of response (DoR) was 5.0 months, and the median PFS was 7.3 months. Based on these results, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted accelerated approval to infigratinib on 28 May 2021. The phase III randomized confirmatory study PROOF 301, which was required to gain full FDA approval, compared infigratinib to standard-of-care gemcitabine plus cisplatin in the first-line treatment of patients with unresectable or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2 gene fusions or other rearrangements (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03773302). The study was terminated early due to poor accrual, but the results reported here provide valuable lessons for the future development and evaluation of FGFR inhibitors.

sec.title: Study patients
sec.p: Adult patients with confirmed histologically or cytologically unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 gene fusion or rearrangement were eligible for inclusion. Testing for FGFR2 rearrangement could be carried out locally or by a central laboratory next-generation sequencing assay (FoundationOne CDx®, Foundation Medicine, Cambridge, MA). The AmoyDx® Comprehensive Panel (Amoy Diagnostics Co., Ltd, Shanghai, China) was used for FGFR2 molecular determination in China.

Eligible patients required adequate hepatic, renal, and bone marrow function as follows: total bilirubin ≤1.5 × the upper limit of normal (ULN) unless documented Gilbert’s syndrome is present; serum transaminases ≤2.5 × ULN (≤5 × ULN if metastatic liver disease present); creatinine clearance ≥45 ml/min; amylase/lipase ≤2.0 × ULN; absolute neutrophil count ≥1.0 × 109/l; platelet count ≥100 × 109/l; hemoglobin ≥9.0 g/dl; inorganic phosphorus and total corrected serum calcium levels within normal limits. An Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group26 performance status of 0 or 1 was required.

Patients with gall-bladder or ampulla of Vater carcinoma were excluded. Prior systemic anticancer therapy for unresectable, locally advanced, or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma was not allowed, except for neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy that was completed >6 months before the first dose of the study drug. To enhance accrual, the study was later amended to permit a gemcitabine-based chemotherapy for less than or equal to one cycle. Other exclusion criteria included prior liver transplantation, history of mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase or selective FGFR inhibitor use, corneal or retinal disorder confirmed via ophthalmic examination, history of extensive tissue calcification, concurrent use of medications increasing serum phosphorus or calcium concentration, or moderate or strong inducers or inhibitors of CYP3A4.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: The PROOF 301 study design has been previously reported27 and is provided in the complete protocol in Supplementary Appendix S1, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.106306. This multicenter, open-label, randomized, controlled phase III study aimed to determine whether first-line treatment with infigratinib improved PFS assessed by BICR (primary objective) and overall survival (OS; key secondary objective) compared with gemcitabine plus cisplatin in patients with unresectable or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements.

Secondary endpoints included investigator-determined PFS, overall response rate, best overall response, disease control rate, DoR, and the type, frequency, and severity of adverse events. The adverse events of special interest were potential drug-induced liver injury; retinal detachment of grade ≥3, regardless of relationship to study drug; keratitis grade ≥3 with suspected relationship to study drug; pathological fractures potentially related or related to metastatic tumor to bone and/or study drug; vascular calcifications accompanied by ischemic adverse events; or overdose (≥200 mg of infigratinib) associated with an adverse event potentially related to study drug. An independent data monitoring committee oversaw study safety. This study adhered to the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use Guideline for Good Clinical Practice, local regulations (including European Directive 2001/20/EC and US Code of Federal Regulations Title 21), and the Declaration of Helsinki.

Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a 2 : 1 ratio to receive oral infigratinib 125 mg on days 1-21 of a 28-day treatment cycle or to intravenous gemcitabine (1000 mg/m2) + cisplatin (25 mg/m2) on days 1 and 8 of a 21-day cycle as per the labeling and local institutional practices. Stratification factors included disease stage, geographic region, prior neoadjuvant/adjuvant treatment, and one prior cycle of gemcitabine-based chemotherapy.
Radiographic evaluation was planned for every 8 weeks ±7 days from the first dose of study drug for tumor response [Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST) v1.1].28

Patients who discontinued the study drug for radiographic progressive disease by RECIST v1.1 criteria confirmed by BICR were to be followed up approximately every 3 months (via telephone or office visit) for survival status and new anticancer therapy information (subsequent therapy and progression/PFS2) until the end of the study. Patients who discontinued for other reasons were to continue to have radiographic assessments every 8 weeks ±7 days until centrally confirmed radiographic progressive disease. Thereafter, these patients were to be followed up approximately every 3 months, as described earlier. Patients in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin arm could cross over to infigratinib following BICR radiographic progressive disease and recheck of the exclusion criteria, and were followed for safety, PFS2, and OS.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The primary endpoint was median PFS as assessed by BICR. A PFS hazard ratio of 0.67 was targeted based on an assumed median PFS of 11.9 with infigratinib versus 8.0 months with gemcitabine and cisplatin.4 With a planned 2 : 1 randomization, 228 PFS events were required among a target accrual of ∼300 patients to provide 80% power to determine whether infigratinib improved median PFS compared with chemotherapy at a two-sided significance level of 0.05.

The end of the study was defined as the time when 224 OS events had been reached (for the primary OS analysis) and the last patient had completed study treatment. The primary efficacy analyses were conducted on the intention-to-treat population, defined as all patients who were randomized, regardless of whether they initiated treatment. Patients were analyzed according to their randomized treatment group assignment. In general, categorical variables were summarized using counts and percent. Continuous variables were summarized using number of patients, mean, median, standard deviation, Q1, Q3, minimum, and maximum. Time to event endpoints (i.e. PFS, OS, and DoR) were analyzed by the Kaplan–Meier method. Due to early termination of the study by the sponsors, no inferential tests were conducted. The data analysis was carried out using SAS software, version 9.4 or later (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC).

sec.title: Patients
sec.p:
Between 6 June 2019 and 7 October 2022 (study termination), 1127 patients completed molecular pre-screening across 120 sites as part of this clinical trial. Among the pre-screened population, 1049 (93.0%) patients were excluded due to the absence of FGFR2 fusion/rearrangement (n = 822; 72.9%), or other reasons (n = 227; 20.1%), including lack of tumor sample, insufficient or poor-quality sample, or physician and/or patient decision to withdraw. An FGFR2 rearrangement was identified by local or central testing in a total of 77 (6.8%) pre-screened patients (Figure 1).Figure 1
CONSORT diagram. FGFR, fibroblast growth factor receptor.

Among these, 63 patients were further assessed for enrollment eligibility, and 15 patients were deemed ineligible. A total of 48 (4.3% of the pre-screened population) patients were randomly assigned to treatment: 29 to the infigratinib group and 19 to the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group. Two patients assigned to the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group withdrew from the study before receiving treatment. Patient demographics and disease characteristics were generally balanced between the treatment groups (Table 1). The study was terminated early by the sponsor due to the high rate of screen failure, low enrollment, and unlikely feasibility of timely completion of this confirmatory study. The protocol was updated to allow one cycle of chemotherapy, in order to enhance accrual, although assessment of whether this led to improved accrual rates was not feasible due to the early termination of the study, with only two patients recruited in this category. Consequently, further development and commercialization of infigratinib in oncology were stopped, and the sponsor voluntarily requested withdrawal of the approval for infigratinib for previously treated, unresectable, locally advanced, or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 fusion or other rearrangement, which the FDA announced on 16 May 2024. Due to the limited sample size achieved, the data presented do not have the power for comparison between arms. A summary of the efficacy and safety data in the accrued population is provided.

sec.title: Central confirmation of FGFR2 fusion or other rearrangement
sec.p: Tissue samples from a total of 846 patients were evaluated by the central laboratory next-generation sequencing assay. The rate of sample failure was 15% (n = 131), primarily due to low tumor content and contamination. Passing and qualified samples (n = 725) were obtained from 529 and 196 patients, respectively. An FGFR2 fusion or other rearrangement was present in 48 (6.6%) patients. Other oncogenic or likely oncogenic alterations that were detected by the central assay at a rate of ≥ 2% are presented in Supplementary Appendix S2, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.106306.

sec.title: Secondary endpoints
sec.p: The estimated PFS rate at 6 months was 64.9% (95% CI 41.6% to 80.8%) for infigratinib and 59.9% (95% CI 28.4% to 81.2%) in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group, and at 12 months was 32.5% (95% CI 7.9% to 60.8%) and 29.9% (95% CI 5.2% to 61.2%), for the infigratinib and gemcitabine plus cisplatin groups, respectively. The investigator-assessed median PFS was 7.4 months [19 events overall (65.5%), all with disease progression; 95% CI 5.7-9.2 months] in the infigratinib group and 5.2 months [eight events overall (42.1%), all with disease progression; 95% CI 3.7 months-NE] in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group (Figure 2B, Table 2). The investigator-assessed estimated PFS rates at 6 months were 65.6% (95% CI 44.2% to 80.4%) in the infigratinib group and 45.9% (95% CI 18.0% to 70.2%) in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group, and at 12 months were 19.4% (95% CI 5.9% to 38.8%) and 30.6% (95% CI 6.2% to 60.4%) for the infigratinib and the gemcitabine plus cisplatin groups, respectively.

Objective response assessed by BICR was 37.9% (95% CI 20.7% to 57.7%) of patients in the infigratinib group and 15.8% (95% CI 3.4% to 39.6%) of patients in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group, all of which were a partial response (Table 2). Median DoR was 5.6 months (95% CI 3.7 months-NE) in the infigratinib group and NE (95% CI 3.9 months-NE) in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group. The disease control rate was 86.2% (95% CI 68.3% to 96.1%) and 73.7% (95% CI 48.8% to 90.9%) for the infigratinib and gemcitabine plus cisplatin groups, respectively.

The investigator-assessed confirmed objective response rate was 31.0% (95% CI 15.3% to 50.8%) for patients in the infigratinib group and 10.5% (95% CI 1.3% to 33.1%) for patients in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group, all of which were a partial response (Table 2). Median investigator-assessed DoR was 7.5 months (95% CI 3.7 months-NE) in the infigratinib group and NE (95% CI 8.1 months-NE) in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group. Investigator-assessed disease control rate was 96.6% (95% CI 82.2% to 99.9%) and 73.7% (95% CI 48.8% to 90.9%) for the infigratinib and gemcitabine plus cisplatin groups, respectively.

At data cut-off, eight (27.6%) patients in the infigratinib group and three (15.8%) in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group had died. In the infigratinib group, six patients died due to progressive disease and two died due to other reasons (one unknown, one stroke secondary to metastatic disease). All three patients in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group died due to progressive disease. Median OS was NE in both groups (Figure 2C, Table 2). The estimated OS rates were 96.4% (95% CI 77.2% to 99.5%) for infigratinib and 92.3% (95% CI 56.6% to 98.9%) for gemcitabine plus cisplatin at 6 months; 77.7% (95% CI 54.0% to 90.2%) and 71.9% (95% CI 34.2% to 90.4%) at 12 months; and 55.6% (95% CI 28.7% to 76.0%) and 71.9% (95% CI 34.2% to 90.4%) at 24 months, respectively.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: All 29 patients in the infigratinib group and 17 patients in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group received at least one dose of their assigned treatment, with the median (range) duration of treatment being 6.5 months (0.6-22.7 months) and 4.4 months (1.6-13.3 months), respectively. The median (range) number of cycles received by the infigratinib group was 7.0 (0-24) with a relative dose intensity of 100% (77%-100%). In the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group, the median (range) number of cycles was 7.0 (2-19) with a relative dose intensity of 100% (92%-100%), for both gemcitabine and cisplatin, respectively.

Adverse events are summarized in Table 3 and Supplementary Appendix S3, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.106306. Grade 3-4 adverse events occurred in 23 (79.3%) patients in the infigratinib group and 10 (58.8%) patients in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group. The most common grade 3-4 adverse events in the infigratinib group were increased alanine aminotransferase [3 (10.3%)], increased aspartate aminotransferase [3 (10.3%)], and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia syndrome [3 (10.3%)]. The most common grade 3-4 adverse events in the chemotherapy group were neutropenia [5 (29.4%)] and anemia [2 (11.8%)]. Study treatment was discontinued due to adverse events in seven (24.1%) patients in the infigratinib group and four (23.5%) patients in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group. Dose reduction due to adverse events occurred in 19 (65.5%) patients in the infigratinib group and 8 (47.1%) patients in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group. The most common treatment-related adverse events in the infigratinib group were hyperphosphatemia (82.8%), alopecia (41.4%), palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia syndrome (41.4%), fatigue (37.9%), diarrhea (37.9%), dry eye (37.9%), stomatitis (34.5%), decreased appetite (31.0%), arthralgia (27.6%), and dry mouth (27.6%). The most common treatment-related adverse events in the gemcitabine plus cisplatin group were nausea (58.8%), fatigue (47.1%), anemia (29.4%), and asthenia (29.4%).Table 3

Three adverse events of special interest occurred in three patients during treatment with infigratinib. One patient experienced a grade 1 pathological fracture considered related to study treatment; the dose of study treatment was not changed, and the event was reported as not resolved. Another patient experienced grade 3 vascular calcifications accompanied by ischemic adverse events, leading to permanent discontinuation of study drug. The event was reported as resolved. A third patient experienced grade 3 keratitis.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The PROOF 301 trial was designed to investigate the oral selective FGFR inhibitor infigratinib in the first-line setting compared with standard-of-care gemcitabine plus cisplatin in patients with unresectable or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring an FGFR2 gene fusion or other rearrangement. This confirmatory trial was enrolling for >3 years after conditional approval before being terminated early due to poor accrual. As a result, inferential statistical analyses could not be carried out. All efficacy and safety outcomes should therefore be interpreted as descriptive, and the study cannot be considered confirmatory of prior phase II findings.

Accordingly, the PROOF 301 trial primarily provides insight into the factors that drove its significant accrual challenges. Firstly, it is not always feasible in rare diseases with rare alterations to efficiently execute a sufficiently powered phase III trial, as the sample size required may be considerably greater than the number of patients eligible for participation in the trial. This concern is compounded when there are other interventional trials actively recruiting the same patient population, as was certainly the case for this study. In ultra-rare conditions, work with regulatory agencies is needed to develop acceptable alternative trial designs such as standard phase II trials complemented by analyses using external control comparators derived from real-world data. Secondly, at the time of study initiation, turnaround times for profiling results in biomarker-driven studies in the first-line setting could extend for many weeks, potentially leading to a delay in treatment initiation. Innovations in cell-free DNA analysis, particularly fusion partner-agnostic methods, are increasing detection rates for FGFR2 fusions, but tissue remains essential for confirmation and comprehensive profiling. Given the modest frequency of FGFR2 fusions in cholangiocarcinoma, both patients and providers may have been reluctant to wait due to disease-related and/or psychological factors. Thirdly, the standard of care for advanced BTC changed during the recruitment period, so the lack of immunotherapy in the control arm may have made this arm less attractive. Fourthly, the recruitment period overlapped substantially with the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, which may have further complicated clinical trial enrollment during this period. Fifthly, and key, the real-world prevalence of FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement in treatment-naive cholangiocarcinoma may be lower than expected, as it was 6.8% among >1100 patients screened in our study compared with the 9%-16% rate usually reported for cholangiocarcinomas.9,13,15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 This low rate may be partly due to the high failure rate of profiling assays and dilution of the prevalence due to inclusion of patients with extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. A biological reason may be that FGFR2 fusions are enriched in the refractory setting as these indolent tumors often allow for more lines of therapy. A sixth and encouraging reason for low accrual may be that more treatment options have become available for these patients, including additional FGFR inhibitors, which may have influenced treatment sequencing decisions for patients and oncologists. While not all patients ultimately receive later-line therapy and cross-over in this study was limited, the availability of these options may none the less have factored into enrollment decisions during the accrual period, including a preference to defer treatment with an FGFR inhibitor to a subsequent line with their local oncologist instead of traveling for a first-line trial.

Nevertheless, the lessons from PROOF 301 highlight several potential solutions for increasing accrual to future biomarker-selected trials in cholangiocarcinoma. Firstly, for technological advancement, tumor profiling assays that require less analyte stand to decrease technical failure rates, which currently range from 15% to 27%.13 Secondly, liquid biopsies may add value where solid tumor biopsies fail, but performance of these assays can vary for detection of FGFR2 fusions, so understanding the false-negative rate of the assay is important.29 Thirdly, improved multidisciplinary collaboration between oncology, interventional radiology, pathology, and clinical trial staff can improve yield from biopsies and decrease turnaround time, as shown recently for epidermal growth factor receptor mutation testing in lung cancer.30,31 Fourthly, further education and outreach to patient and clinician communities to emphasize the importance of widespread and early tumor profiling may increase the number of patients matched with clinical trials and also with many currently approved targeted therapies. However, despite these approaches to improve recruitment efforts, the poor accrual of this study highlights the challenge of accruing randomized clinical trials in biomarker-selected subpopulations of rare tumors. Upfront molecular profiling of resected high-risk cholangiocarcinomas could enhance trial recruitment for first-line biomarker-driven trials for patients with recurrent disease.

The experience of this study also raises questions regarding paths to full approval in this setting. Creative approaches such as accepting single arm, phase II clinical trial data demonstrating sufficiently robust efficacy, novel clinical trial design for pivotal trials, consideration of common control arm studies, and/or analysis of real-world data may provide alternatives to large, randomized trials in special circumstances. Furthermore, this trial with a target accrual of ∼300 patients would have taken >15 years given the enrollment of 48 patients in 3 years. Even with a 10% enrollment rate, ∼3000 patients would have needed to be screened. Randomized studies that require many years to complete may continue to have difficulty with accrual in a rare cancer like cholangiocarcinoma with a rapidly shifting treatment landscape. Umbrella trials using a shared control arm offer an efficient solution for studying rare genomic alterations (like FGFR2 fusions), but require careful consideration of feasibility, power, and analytic interpretation.

Infigratinib and pemigatinib, both second-generation, reversible, pan-FGFR inhibitors, previously received conditional approval by the FDA for pretreated patients with cholangiocarcinoma and FGFR2 fusion or other rearrangement.32,33 Futibatinib is the first third-generation, irreversible, pan-FGFR inhibitor approved by the FDA in the same setting with numerically higher survival and response rates.34,35 As next-generation inhibitors with improved efficacy gain approval, control arms in ongoing studies risk becoming obsolete, underscoring the need for innovative trial designs and flexible regulatory pathways that can adapt to the realities of limited patient populations and rapidly evolving standards of care in rare, molecularly defined cancers.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In conclusion, although early termination and poor accrual limit the interpretability of the efficacy and safety outcomes, the experience from PROOF 301 informs the design and conduct of future biomarker-selected clinical trials. Despite the discontinuation of the development and commercialization of infigratinib in oncology, two other FGFR inhibitors (pemigatinib and futibatinib) remain available to patients in the United States and the European Union through accelerated FDA and conditional European Medicines Agency approvals in the refractory setting. However, the confirmatory phase III trial of pemigatinib versus first-line gemcitabine plus cisplatin (NCT03656536) and the confirmatory phase III trial of futibatinib with a similar design (NCT04093362) were both terminated due to poor enrollment.

The treatment options for patients with FGFR-altered cholangiocarcinoma will likely expand in the future as additional FGFR inhibitors are showing positive early data (erdafitinib, derazantinib, lirafugratinib, tinengotinib), and others are in development (KIN-3248, TYRA-200, CPL-304110). As new targeted therapies demonstrate clinical benefit for patients with cholangiocarcinoma and other rare cancers, we support continued partnership with regulatory agencies to develop creative paths to approval for our patients.
